The competing review wanted to fail it, but its objections did not hold up: the criteria it called 'doing too much at once' are really just single checks over one requested set of files or one cautious-handling instruction, which is allowed; its claim that certain checks were filed under the wrong category cited a grading rule that does not actually exist in this project's guidelines; and the one remaining concern (a slightly low share of negative criteria) is only advisory and never fails a task. scenario: A landlord's tenant (Pemberton) moved out and left the unit a mess, and the landlord still holds the $2,800 deposit. They asked the assistant to look at three damage photos, list the repair, cleaning, and renovation jobs, assign each to the right contractor, draft a text to each contractor, and run an ROI using the 0.7% price-to-rent rule and two CSV files to decide between a standard fix and a premium renovation, then write up the math and update memory.
did: A correct response had to inspect the photos to build the task list, assign and draft contractor messages, compute the standard-versus-premium ROI from the provided cost data, flag any single fix over $500 for sign-off, and record the unit status, portfolio debt, and risk to memory, all while honestly handling the property identity details the prompt never actually supplied.
why: This rubric fails. Four criteria are scored backwards because they punish a correct response. The property name, unit, and full address (Barton Creek Villas / Unit 301 / 2800 Barton Creek Blvd) appear nowhere the agent could reach, so an honest agent must either ask for them or use a placeholder; yet one criterion penalizes asking for the address, a second penalizes using a placeholder, and a third rewards a specific debt figure ($38,200) that cannot be derived from anything the agent was given. A fourth criterion penalizes the agent for assuming a premium-rent uplift, even though the prompt demands a premium-tier ROI and the only cost file provided gives premium costs but no rent uplift, so that assumption is unavoidable and the criterion contradicts two other criteria that reward the finished ROI. On top of that, one more criterion requires exactly eight repair tasks when the prompt names no number and the photos reasonably support a range, so a response listing six or ten valid tasks would be wrongly marked down (a smaller defect that does not by itself fail the task). There is also a second, independent reason to fail: the unit tests hard-code that same unsupported property identity and demand a literal 'URGENT: OWNER SIGN-OFF REQUIRED' header the prompt never asks for, so the tests wrongly fail a correct response. For the record, the competing review's claim that the answer was leaked in an input file is wrong, because that file was not in the workspace the agent could actually read.
fix: Rewrite the address, placeholder, and debt criteria so they no longer punish the only honest responses to missing data: reward either asking for the property details or clearly marking them as placeholders, and drop the fixed $38,200 debt value (instead reward a debt figure correctly derived from the data the agent actually has). Change the premium-rent criterion so it stops penalizing the rent-uplift assumption the ROI requires; if an uplift figure is wanted, supply it in the input data. Replace the exact-eight-tasks requirement with a range or with 'identifies the major repair, cleaning, and renovation tasks.' Fix the unit tests to stop asserting the unsupported Barton Creek identity and the unrequired sign-off header.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

The five question answers and the credit-card numbers are all graded correctly against the question sheet and the connected-account data. The competing review's attempt to fail it on contrived inputs and on a miscategorization rule did not hold: the slides really are course slides and the graded question sheet really is a photo, and the cited grading rule does not exist in this project's guidelines.

Loosen the memory criterion to accept the memory file saved anywhere reasonable (such as a memory folder), rather than requiring the workspace top level.

scenario: Someone trying to build muscle wants variety in the animal-meat sources across their meals. They uploaded photos of five recent meals and asked the assistant to count, for each meal, how many different animal-meat sources it contains, add those per-meal counts into a total, then write a plan.md with that total, the exact average per meal, and a two-week checklist (week one aiming for double the average, week two for triple), plus their May 30 active energy at the end.
did: A correct response had to look at each meal photo, tally the distinct animal-meat sources per meal, report the total and the exact per-meal average, build the two-week doubling/tripling checklist, and append the May 30 active energy figure.
why: This rubric fails. Two criteria pin an exact answer to a count that is genuinely a judgment call from busy food photos, so a careful, reasonable response would be wrongly failed. The number of distinct meats is contestable: the loaded pizza alone can reasonably be read as anywhere from two to four different meats (chorizo or pepperoni, sausage, ham or bacon, possible chicken), and the roast as one or two, so a fair total spans roughly five to eight. One criterion locks the total at exactly six and another locks the average at exactly 1.2; a defensible tally of five meats giving a 1.0 average, which is what a capable vision-equipped run actually produced, would fail both. Because these are two separate reported values (the total and the average), they count as two distinct over-pinned criteria, which together cross the fail line. The doubling and tripling criteria were not counted, since those operations are exactly what the prompt asks for and only inherit the same underlying ambiguity. The competing review rated this acceptable only because it took six as given and never re-examined whether the count was contestable.
fix: Stop pinning a single exact value on a contestable visual count. Either accept a defensible range for the total and the average (for example, total of five to eight and the matching average), or reward any per-meal tally that the response justifies from the photos, rather than requiring exactly six and 1.2. If a single ground-truth count is truly intended, use meal photos where the number of distinct meats is unambiguous.
agree: No — I'm stricter here; the second opinion lets it pass.

The image shows the #1 counter first reading zero at the 3:15 row (there is no 3:25 row on the page at all), but one criterion rewards saying it first hits zero at 3:25 and explicitly penalizes the correct 3:15. The other planted-error checks were verified correct. The competing review missed this because it only looked at structure and a typo and never checked these two values against the actual pixels.
fix: Correct both gold values to match the scan: change the first-zero criterion to reward the 3:15 reading (and stop penalizing it), and change the duration criterion to reward roughly fifteen minutes rather than five. scenario: Someone is going back and forth with a client on a skincare ad creative and wants a second pair of eyes before the next review round. They dropped a ZIP with the ad mockup image and the campaign spec sheet and asked the assistant to check three things: whether the background and layout match the brand guidelines, whether the claims on the left of the layout hold up against what the preview on the right actually shows, and whether any leftover placeholder or draft strings remain in the graphic, then save a structured review as ad_design_audit.md and overwrite MEMORY.md with progress and open items.

why: This rubric does not fail, but it has two small defects. Every visual detail it checks is verified correct against the mockup, and the criterion that penalizes wrongly passing the unsupported 'family in the photo with kids' claim is scored the right way (it penalizes the wrong call, not the correct one). The first defect is a redundant pair: one criterion rewards noticing that the testimonial photo is too small to show an identifiable family with kids, and another penalizes rating that same left-side claim as passing, so the two criteria really grade the same single decision and are counted once. Both are minor and together stay below the fail line. There was no leftover-from-an-old-version or fabricated-input problem, and the prompt explicitly says to overwrite MEMORY.md, so there is no filename ambiguity.
fix: Merge the redundant pair so the small-testimonial-photo observation and the penalty for passing that same claim are handled by a single criterion. Reframe the image-reading criterion as a positive check that rewards reading or rendering the mockup before drafting the audit, rather than penalizing its absence.

did: A correct response had to produce all three files grounded in what the footage actually shows, recommend a final cut that stays under 20 seconds, keep the sponsor mention only if the video supports it, avoid overclaiming weak footage, and base the thumbnail on the provided references.
why: This rubric has three problems but it does not fail the task. First, the user twice states the recommended cut must come in under 20 seconds, yet no criterion actually checks that ceiling (the related checks only verify the edit is internally consistent and that captions line up, so a 22-second plan would still pass), and the placeholder test file does not cover it either. Second, C22 and C26 grade the exact same decision about not inventing unrelated stock photos or sponsor logos, just from opposite directions, so they double up on one thing; this counts as a single redundancy. Third, the user spells out valid subtitle formatting (numbered cues, proper timestamps, non-overlapping ranges, blank lines), but no criterion checks that formatting. Counted against all 28 checks, these add up to too few to fail the task. The second-opinion review wanted to fail it, but its case leaned on checks that merely describe how the agent should work and on complaints about checks that actually mirror the user's own follow-up instructions, none of which hold up; stripped of those, its real concerns match this same verdict. Every footage-based detail was confirmed against the frame analysis and both reference images.
fix: Add a criterion that the recommended final cut is under 20 seconds. Merge C22 and C26 into one check on the forbidden-asset rule so the single decision is not scored twice. Add a criterion that the caption file uses valid subtitle formatting: numbered cues, HH:MM:SS,mmm timestamps, non-overlapping ranges, and blank lines between cues.
agree: No — the second opinion flags it, but on a closer look the concern doesn't hold up.

scenario: A student is closing out an understory field lab for their professor, due Tuesday morning. They dropped in all the files and a spec, and asked the assistant to work through the spec: read species richness, garlic mustard counts, and deer-browse severity straight from the plot photos before trusting the typed logs, fix everything in order in a CSV, write a report and plot_observations.csv, email the professor about any plot needing follow-up, message a collaborator if the slope plot disagrees, log three plots in a tracker, block out their Monday write-up time and set a submission reminder from a screenshot, note the sources in MEMORY.md, and say what to redo.
did: A correct response had to read the three measurements from each plot photo (overriding the typed logs where they conflict), build plot_observations.csv and the report to the spec, rank the plots by richness, handle the email, message, tracker, calendar, and reminder steps, and keep a MEMORY.md source log.
why: This rubric has a few gaps but it does not fail the task. Three required pieces are not checked by any criterion: the content of the MEMORY.md source log, the CSV's visit_order column (which the spec says to derive from photo timestamps while ignoring a planted guess column), and the CSV's needs_followup column with its conditional rules. These are real coverage gaps, but they are secondary pieces and, under this project's guidance, missing-coverage gaps are treated as advisory and do not by themselves fail a task. None of the checks that were written are wrong: the reviewer opened all three plot photos and confirmed the richness, garlic mustard, and browse values, confirmed the slope and valley plots correctly contradict their typed logs, and confirmed the richness-first health ranking is spec-faithful even though the valley plot has invasives. The second-opinion review wanted to fail this, but its case rested on the rubric having no point-deducting checks (a style preference, not a defect) and on one claim that a key trap was unguarded, which is false: existing positive checks already catch a response that copies the wrong typed value. With no incorrect written checks, the task does not fail; it lands just short of clean because of the three coverage gaps.
fix: Add a criterion checking MEMORY.md content (one line per uploaded file mapping it to its deliverable or cross-check role). Add a criterion that the CSV's visit_order is derived from the photo timestamps (earliest = 1) and not copied from the planted guess column. Add a criterion verifying the CSV's needs_followup column against the spec's rules (yes when garlic mustard is at least 3, when a plot's typed log doesn't match, or when the slope plot shows visible invasives despite a no-match log).

scenario: The user has spent months building a home studio and just finished an acoustic treatment, taking before-and-after sound-level readings at several spots and sketching where the panels were placed. They ask the assistant to pull everything in the workspace together into one documented report and save it as studio_treatment_report.md.
did: A correct response had to read the handwritten notebook images and the order emails, then produce the report in the required format with correct computed numbers: the per-position level averages and overall reduction, the cost per dB of improvement based only on the treatment materials cost, and the right next-phase recommendation tied to whether the average reduction reaches 8 dB.
why: This rubric does not fail the task, but it has real gaps. Every one of the 10 written criteria is correct and well grounded: they accurately check the readings against the photos and confirm the assistant looked up and used the actual purchase records, and the order-confirmation email for the Auralex 12-pack at $187 matches the criterion exactly, so those checks are sound. The genuine weakness is that the rubric only checks the assistant's working steps and never checks the report's final computed numbers. Three things go unchecked: the cost per dB of improvement (which had to use the $187 treatment cost, not the $1,165 total studio spend, and the assistant in fact got it wrong), the next-phase recommendation (the average reduction was 7.2 dB, under 8, so the report should recommend more frequency testing rather than ceiling treatment), and the stated average levels in the report (the assistant's figures were off versus the correct pre 81.5 / post 74.3 / reduction 7.2). The first two are significant gaps because they are core computed results; the third is a smaller gap because one existing criterion touches the averages indirectly. None of these gaps, however, counts as a reason to fail the rubric: a missing check is treated as advice to add coverage, not as a failure of the checks that are present. So the rubric passes despite leaving the report's key outputs unverified.
fix: Add a criterion that checks the report's cost per dB of improvement is correct and based only on the treatment materials cost (about $25.97 from $187 / 7.2 dB), not the total studio investment. Add a criterion that checks the next-phase recommendation matches the rule, recommending further frequency testing because the 7.2 dB average is below 8 dB. Add a criterion that checks the report states the correct average pre-treatment level, post-treatment level, and overall reduction (81.5 / 74.3 / 7.2).
agree: No — the second opinion flags it, but on a closer look the concern doesn't hold up.

scenario: The user is cleaning up Adrian's Willow Creek field-lab packet before a Monday deadline and has uploaded the creek photos, a notebook page, Marcus's notes, a site index, the protocol/spec, a roster, and a deadline screenshot. They ask the assistant to turn it all into the final submission packet, handle anything that needs logging or follow-up, and warn that one photo may be from a different trip and Marcus's notes may be unreliable, so the assistant should sanity-check the real evidence rather than just copy his guesses.
did: A correct response had to read the photos and notebook, build the report, observations CSV, and memory note, log and flag the real field issues (the ocean photo excluded, the algae-covered and iron-stained sites, Site C's low dissolved oxygen and questionable pH), update the tracker, email Dr. Park, block the write-up time from the screenshot, and rank the three sites by water quality from the evidence rather than Marcus's guess.
why: This rubric does not fail the task. All 18 written criteria are correct and well grounded: they accurately check the site classifications against the photos, correctly exclude the ocean shot, correctly require follow-up for Site C's low dissolved oxygen, and correctly penalize recording the questionable pH 8.4 as if it were clean across the CSV, report, memory note, and tracker. None of these checks wrongly punish a correct answer, and the negative-weight checks are aimed at the genuinely bad action, so they are sound. The platform's second review was empty for this task, so there was nothing to reconcile against. The two real gaps are both about missing coverage rather than broken checks. First, the headline correction of the whole task is the water-quality ranking: the spec requires a quality_rank in the CSV, a ranking section in the report, and the rank in the tracker row, and the evidence overturns Marcus by making Site A best and Site C worst, yet no criterion and none of the 10 real tests check that the ranking exists or is ordered correctly. Second, the rubric thoroughly checks Site B and Site C but never checks any of Site A's own measured values, only that its row exists. The ranking gap is significant and the Site A gap is smaller because Site A is the uneventful control. Neither gap counts as a reason to fail the rubric, since a missing check is treated as advice to add coverage, not as a failure of the checks that are present.
fix: Add a criterion that checks the assistant produced the water-quality ranking in all three places the spec requires (the CSV quality_rank column, the report ranking section, and the tracker row) and that it ranks Site A as 1 (best), Site B as 2, and Site C as 3 based on the evidence rather than Marcus's guess. Add criteria checking Site A's own values the way Site B and C are checked: clear turbidity, pH 7.2, dissolved oxygen 9.2, and no visible issues.
agree: Yes — both agree it holds up.
